summary.text: Euler's formula says the complex exponential function is eⁱˣ = cos x + i sin x, tying exponentials to trigonometry.
It appears throughout mathematics, physics, chemistry and engineering, and Richard Feynman called it the most remarkable formula in mathematics.
Euler derived it around 1740 by comparing series expansions of the exponential and trigonometric expressions, and it was first published in 1748.

paragraphs.heading: What the formula says
paragraphs.text: Euler's formula ties the trigonometric functions to the complex exponential function. For any real number x, it states that eⁱˣ = cos x + i sin x. Here e stands for the base of the natural logarithm, i for the imaginary unit, and cos and sin for the cosine and sine functions. The right-hand side is sometimes written cis x, short for cosine plus i sine.

paragraphs.heading: Why people prize it
paragraphs.text: The formula turns up everywhere in mathematics, physics, chemistry and engineering. The physicist Richard Feynman called it "our jewel" and "the most remarkable formula in mathematics". It also stays true when x is a complex number, and it keeps the name Euler's formula in that wider case.

paragraphs.heading: Walking round a circle
paragraphs.text: As φ runs through the real numbers, e^iφ traces out the unit circle in the complex plane, so it is always a unit complex number. Here φ is the angle, measured counterclockwise in radians, between the positive real axis and a line from the origin to the point on the circle. Setting the angle to π gives e^iπ = −1. Written as e^iπ + 1 = 0, this is known as Euler's identity.

paragraphs.heading: How it was found
paragraphs.text: In 1714 the English mathematician Roger Cotes gave a geometric argument which, once a misplaced factor of √(−1) is corrected, reads i x = ln (cos x + i sin x). Exponentiating both sides of that equation gives Euler's formula. Around 1740, Leonhard Euler turned to the exponential function and found the formula by setting the series expansions of exponential and trigonometric expressions side by side. It first appeared in print in 1748, in his foundational treatise Introductio in analysin infinitorum.

paragraphs.heading: Logarithms with many values
paragraphs.text: Cotes's logarithm version is not always correct for complex numbers, because a complex logarithm can take infinitely many values, which differ by multiples of 2πi. Euler himself suggested that complex logarithms have infinitely many values. Letters between Euler and Johann Bernoulli show that Bernoulli did not fully understand them. Euler's formula can in fact be used to define the complex logarithm: writing z = |z| e^iφ for any z ≠ 0 leads to ln z = ln |z| + i φ.

paragraphs.heading: A short proof
paragraphs.text: One proof looks at f(θ) = e^(−iθ) (cos θ + i sin θ) for real values of θ, which is the trigonometric side divided by the exponential side. It shows that this quotient never changes, and since f(0) = 1/1 = 1, it equals 1 for every real θ. So the two sides must be equal: e^iθ = cos θ + i sin θ. Dividing is allowed because the exponential function is never zero.
